articles.headline: Leeds United v Manchester United: Premier League – live
keyFacts: Leeds United face rivals Manchester United in the Premier League, with Ethan Ampadu captaining Leeds for the 100th time.
A Leeds victory would lift them to fifth, while Manchester United are experiencing their worst league start in 40 years.
Team news will be announced shortly before the match kicks off at 2pm BST.
body: Leeds’ Ethan Ampadu, who captains the club for the 100th time, speaks to Sky Sports:
We know what this game means. We know that they are not too happy at the moment but we know that they might show a reaction. But we know what we need to do to win this game.
With apologies to Brighton and Palace fans, welcome to the game of the weekend, in the Premier League at least.

Today’s clash between two Uniteds is dripping with narrative and consequence, not least because they are two of the biggest, most historic rivals in England. Leeds have enjoyed a fine start to the season and will leapfrog Liverpool into fifth with victory today while Manchester United are enduring their worst league start in 40 years, with manager Michael Carrick under severe pressure to save his job. The former midfielder has been fighting fires all week after Lisandro Martínez poured petrol on the club’s Champions League defeat in midweek with his post-match incendiary comments about the club’s hierarchy and a lack of investment – remarks for which he has now apologised, sort of.

Carrick has attempted to smooth things over, claiming things are all resolved between player and Manchester United’s director of football Jason Wilcox, and confirmed that Martínez is in the squad for the trip to Elland Road; the 5ft9in centre back will be hoping to do a whole lot better against Dominic Calvert-Lewin than he did against another Dominic in Tottenham’s Solanke, with the latter bullying Martínez to score a late equaliser for 10-man Spurs at Old Trafford next week. If Martínez wants the squad to be improved, he might find himself on the chopping block, the Argentinian’s contract expires at the end of this season, although Manchester United do have an option to end it by another 12 months.

Leeds will be desperate to compound Manchester United’s misery but have not beaten their rivals on their own patch in over 24 years. It was another Manchester United centre back that endured a tough time that day in September 2002, with Rio Ferdinand booed every time he touched the ball following his after his move across the Pennines, before the former Leeds defender lost Harry Kewell for the only goal of the game.
Plenty at stake, then. We’ll have team news for you shortly. Roll on kick-off at 2pm BST.

articles.headline: The dark side of optimizing fertility
keyFacts: Some prospective parents use polygenic screening to test embryos for complex diseases and physical traits, author Kristen V. Brown said.
Most mainstream medical societies and IVF doctors oppose polygenic embryo screening because they believe it lacks value, Brown said.
Embryo editing is currently illegal in the United States and most countries, though interest in the technology is growing, Brown said.
body: A gynecologist points to the head of a fetus in an ultrasound image. | Jan Woitas/picture alliance via Getty Images

We live in an era of endless optimization. Fitness trackers help us measure our lifespan, people are consuming piles of protein in an attempt to be their best selves, and there’s even an urge to maximize our morality . In a world of constant self-improvement, it’s no wonder that journey has reached our attempts at reproduction.

Kristen V. Brown is a journalist and author of the forthcoming book The Immortal Womb: The Centuries-Long Quest to Control the Female Body and Hack Human Reproduction . As the title suggests, she writes about all of the ways people are trying to exert more control over the process of having children.

“I think that what we’re seeing right now is that people will do anything they can to have the healthiest baby possible,” she told Vox. “So much is out of your control, and people are just trying to figure out, how do I get more control? How do I skew the odds in my favor?” She says that one way people try to get more agency is through a technology called PGT-P, or preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic risk.

“If you go through IVF, very often they’ll have you do a basic genetic screening that can detect things like Down syndrome. This screening takes that up a notch,” Brown said. “It uses that same preimplantation genetic testing to look for the likelihood of complex genetic conditions — stuff like heart disease, like diabetes — in order to, quote, ‘let people have the healthiest baby.’”

But what can potential parents do with that knowledge? How far can this technology go? And what are the ethics of using it in the first place? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.

Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Brown, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What other things are they testing embryos for?

For conditions that are only impacted by one gene, like Huntington’s disease, it’s very easy to say, ‘Does this embryo have it or not?’ with a pretty good degree of confidence. But that’s not how this technology works. Something like heart disease, for example, is impacted by hundreds of genes. Also, something like heart disease is not only genetic. It’s affected by environment and lifestyle.

I think that what’s motivating most people is the health aspect. But a lot of these companies are marketing these tests, saying they can also look for height. They can look at eye color. Some of them are promising IQ. How do you even define intelligence, let alone how do you define the genetics of intelligence? Alzheimer’s disease, longevity, which embryo is going to live the longest life. So it’s already gone beyond disease into some of these more aesthetic concerns.
Do we know how many people are doing this?
I think it’s a very small number of people at this point. But I think that we’re seeing more and more companies in the space, and we’re seeing more and more support from fertility doctors.

I want to emphasize that most mainstream medical societies are against this. Most of the IVF doctors I know do not think this has value. Most people in the genetic space do not think this technology has value either for embryos or for adults, but I think we’re seeing support growing.
I think that a lot of people in the fertility space are already envisioning a future where this does become more mainstream because the idea is just so appealing, even if the technology has flaws.
What about embryo editing? Is that something we’re seeing? Can people go in and change things around?

Not right now. Embryo editing is very much illegal in the United States. It is illegal in most countries. How can you be sure enough that it’s safe? Because you won’t know for sure until an embryo grows up into an adult whether anything went awry.

Right now it is illegal, but there is growing interest as the technology has gotten better. Most of the support right now for embryo editing is for disease. The argument for it is that, let’s say you are a carrier for Huntington’s disease or you have Huntington’s disease. Right now, there is something that you can do. You can use polygenic screening to select the embryos that don’t have the disease, but in IVF, even if you don’t have a terrible disease hiding in your DNA, it’s hard to get a lot of embryos.

You have these situations where couples have to do rounds and rounds and rounds of IVF to get one or two embryos that aren’t carriers for a harmful variant, right? And so the argument for it is, let’s give these people a better shot.
But I imagine there are people out there who aren’t looking into editing simply for making children more resistant to diseases. They are looking at those things like eye color and height.

There’s actually a name for that. This tech executive called Brian Armstrong coined this term, the Gattaca stack, [named] after the movie. The vision is to use a suite of fertility technologies to make the perfect human.

The first thing they want to use is this technology called in vitro gametogenesis, which is where you take a skin cell and you turn it into an egg and a sperm, and then you make an embryo with it, so women don’t have to go through rounds of IVF.
The idea is that you can get tons and tons and tons of embryos, and then you can use PGT-P to then screen for the best ones, and then you can use an artificial womb to incubate and grow them.
This brings to mind a certain E word, and that word is eugenics. What are the ethics here?

Because on one hand, I can understand that there are parents who are like, “I just want to have a healthy baby. I want to bring a child into this world. I just want to put my best foot forward with this human that I’m going to bring to Earth.” And then on the other hand, it gets a little weird.

It gets weird fast. In some ways, we’ve already gone down that slippery slope. Right now, even if you don’t go through IVF, we screen against Down syndrome early in pregnancy. Down syndrome is a condition in which you have a disability, but you can live a full, happy, healthy life. For a long time, parents of kids with Down syndrome have argued that already selecting and screening against Down syndrome pregnancies is a form of [eugenics].

As technology gets more advanced, we see that same question applied to more and more conditions. I think that one of the things that we don’t talk about enough is that the genome is complicated. You can’t actually just go in there and be like, ‘I want a tall baby with blue eyes and a great laugh.’

I think that becoming a parent is an exercise in giving up control, and that’s easier for some people than others. I have so much sympathy and empathy for people who are trying to stack the deck. But I think there are just so many variables when it comes to human reproduction that we are never going to be able to fully control the process, as much as we might want to and as appealing as that might sound.

articles.headline: Why are internet upload speeds so much slower than download speeds?
keyFacts: Upload speeds are generally slower than download speeds because most consumers download significantly more data than they upload.
Cable internet providers allocate most copper cable bandwidth to downloads due to physical limitations inherited from one-way television infrastructure.
Fiber internet providers typically offer equal upload and download speeds because optical cables avoid the bandwidth limitations of copper cables.
body: Why are internet upload speeds so much slower than download speeds?
It’s a combination of physical limitations and everyone’s behavior.

If you've checked your home internet plan details or shopped for a new one recently, you might have noticed that the download speeds are far higher than upload speeds. For instance, Xfinity plans in my area currently offer download tiers of 300 Mbps, 500 Mbps and 1 Gbps, but the broadband facts show all three of these plans have the same typical upload speed of 117 Mbps. You'll need to jump to the 2 Gbps plan to see the upload speed increase to around 293 Mbps.
As it turns out, there are a few reasons for this, and modern connections aren't subject to all the same limitations.
The speeds match how most people use the internet

The most pertinent point is a practical matter: Most people download much more than they upload. Almost every way we interact with the internet involves downloading, and what we download is typically much larger than what we upload.

Think about how often you stream video or music compared to uploading it yourself, for instance. Another major download area is installing and updating apps, games and system software, which takes a lot of network bandwidth. Even standard browsing has you download much more data from webpages than the bits of text you upload to log in or post a comment.

Unless you transfer massive files with cloud storage, stream on Twitch or have multiple people taking video calls all day, you probably don't need a fast upload speed. The average person will appreciate having 80 or 90 percent of their bandwidth used to keep downloads quick, rather than having uploads and downloads be roughly equal.
Physical connection limitations

The major reason for slow upload speeds in practice is the limitations of the medium that carries your internet connection. Standard cable internet uses the same coaxial copper lines that were made to deliver cable TV. Obviously, cable TV is a one-way setup where your home almost never needs to communicate back, so cable infrastructure was built around this. But because internet usage requires both up and down communication, internet providers have to decide how much of the limited bandwidth of copper cables to assign to each path. Following what we discussed above, it makes sense to devote the majority of the pipeline to downloads, since that represents most activity.

The Data Over Cable Service Interface Specifications (DOCSIS) standard is what allows internet signals to travel over cables that weren't initially intended for that. Newer versions of this standard improve maximum download and upload speeds, but it costs ISPs a lot of money to install the updated equipment to support it.

Fiber internet, which has light bounce inside a cable instead of electrical signals in twisted wire, doesn't suffer from these problems. Its enormous theoretical bandwidth is far beyond even the best internet speeds today, meaning it has plenty of room to move downloads and uploads at the same speed. That's why fiber providers typically offer equal upload and download speeds.

With cable, it's also common to see slower speeds when everyone in your area is using the internet, since nodes and overall bandwidth are shared across a neighborhood. This isn't a concern with fiber; since it lacks cable's bandwidth limitations, even an entire neighborhood's worth of traffic is not an issue. A fiber connection also sidesteps other issues of copper cables, like interference and electrical noise.
Content delivery networks spread out the work of downloads

Another part of this equation that's not discussed as often is data distribution. Major companies like Netflix and Google use content delivery networks (CDNs) to more quickly deliver downloads all over the world. These are servers designed to more efficiently provide data to people in a certain area, rather than it all coming from a central location.

For instance, if you live in Florida and stream a movie on Netflix, you don't have to download the movie's data from a Netflix HQ server on the West Coast. Instead, Netflix has a network of servers, usually placed near ISP networks for efficiency, that keep copies of the data and deliver it to you (and everyone near you). Downloading something from a server 200 miles away is much faster than pulling from one that's 3,000 miles away and is thus less taxing for the ISP.

However, there's no real equivalent of this for uploads, at least not to the same extent. When you upload something, it needs to travel to its final destination, which could be a server far from where you are. Also, what you're uploading is usually something unique, like backed-up photos or a video you've recorded, so there's no "shortcut" like CDNs provide for thousands of people watching the same movie. The ISP's infrastructure thus has to do much more work to get your uploaded data where it needs to go.

body: Ian Botham reopens war of words with Ben Stokes over Ashes fallout

England lost the last Ashes series 4-1 and Ian Botham criticised England's preparation for the series; Ben Stokes said that 'has-beens' did not have the same factors at play as his England side did when they got ready for the Ashes
Sunday 18 October 2026 13:00, UK
Lord Ian Botham has reopened his war of words with recently retired England captain Ben Stokes.
The pair have criticised each other in the media in the past year following England's poor performance in the Ashes in Australia.
Botham criticised England's lack of preparation ahead of the Ashes series last winter, which led to Stokes calling him and Michael Vaughan "has-beens".

England lost the series 4-1 amid off-the-field issues over late-night drinking sessions and breached curfews.
Botham, who scored 5,200 runs and took 383 wickets in 102 Tests, was asked whether he liked the way Stokes resigned as captain in the middle of a Test match against New Zealand.
"No, I didn't and I stand by what I said," Botham said.
"You have got a situation, starting from the beginning when he had a go at myself and Michael Vaughan in Melbourne because we said they had not prepared properly.
"They played two and a half days of cricket in the build-up to taking on Australia in Perth.
"But to be absolutely honest with you, we had a go at them saying that's ridiculous, no one knows what they are doing, the slip fielders have to practice, very, very difficult."

When Stokes was asked by journalists for his views on the criticisms, he replied: "We've not been preparing for this tour over the last three weeks, we've put a lot of thought and process into this for a few years now.
"There's quite a few factors that play into why we can't prepare how the has-beens maybe prepared in the past."
Botham, who was part of two victorious tours of Australia in 1978-79 and 1986-87, was speaking at the Cheltenham Literature Festival to promote his new book, Seasons.
"So that's open warfare and I'm quite happy with that because I just think he let himself down," Botham said.
"He's a bloody good cricketer and he played well but he let himself down in those final couple of months.
"The team going 2-0 down in Australia, one of them in two days.
"For me to be then seen at Noosa, one of the most popular places in Australia to holiday and, we have got five days off on the lash.
"I just thought that was poor. Curfews, well, they were set and they were broken.
"In the book, I just said that right at the end, a throw away line, 'Well, well, well, Ben Stokes, you are now a member of the has-been team'.
"Didn't go down too well, not that I'm bothered."
Botham said that during the Ashes tour of 1986-87, which England won 2-1, the players would go to Australian wineries to drink and socialise between matches.
"That's out of visual and we were actually winning, so we could have paraded ourselves around a bit if we wanted, but we didn't," Botham added.

articles.headline: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
keyFacts: Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats visiting the West Bank village of Taybeh, injuring a French mayor and damaging a consulate vehicle.
European governments condemned the attack and demanded accountability, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office suggested reports were part of a smear campaign.
Israeli authorities launched investigations into the assault, while Belgium said it will press for European Union sanctions against those responsible.
body: - Published
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys, while France decried the attack as "appalling". Both called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened, suggesting it was part of a "co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".

It was also condemned by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".
In Saturday's incident, the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.

Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice, as well as ensuring the safety of diplomats, journalists and Palestinians.

"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
He also said Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for the violence.
France's Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot echoed those sentiments, calling on Israeli authorities to "urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations".
Poland's foreign affairs ministry also called for a "firm response" from Israeli authorities and for "an end to the spiral of violence in the West Bank".
The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and end the expansion of settlements.

A spokesperson said that while they acknowledged some Israeli officials had condemned the attacks, they said they still expect "full accountability as well as effective measures" to stop the continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.

Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.

But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".

A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."

It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".

Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

articles.headline: America's Dominance in The Game Awards Is Officially Over
keyFacts: United States media representation on The Game Awards 2026 jury dropped to 17 outlets, tying with the United Kingdom.
Multiple American publications left the jury, while Brazil increased its representation to 14 votes.
The Game Awards confirmed that Grand Theft Auto 6 met the eligibility cutoff date.
body: It's been a long time since the U.S. held complete sway over voting in The Game Awards. In 2024 and 2025, American outlets took up just 24 seats on an international jury of more than 130. Since the awards began in 2014, there's been a consistent trend of internationalization as the jury has expanded. Even so, the U.S. has consistently had by far the biggest presence of any single country on the jury — at least 10 more votes than any other nation. But that era is over.

This week, as well as confirming details such as the eligibility cutoff date (yes, as predicted, Grand Theft Auto 6 sneaks in just under the wire), The Game Awards has revealed the composition of the 2026 jury. And the biggest change is the dramatically reduced presence of U.S. media.

There are now just 17 American outlets on the jury, a big drop compared to previous years. At the same time, the U.K. — always the second-biggest power in Game Awards voting — has increased its votes from 14 to 17, drawing level with the U.S. for the first time.

At first, this seems like a symbolic shift, rather than one that will have a meaningful impact on the nominations and winners at the awards. After all, the gaming cultures of the U.S. and U.K. are pretty similar, give or take a FIFA or a Madden. But if you zoom in on the changes to the American voting body, and zoom out to consider changes elsewhere in the jury, it starts to look more significant.

The other story this year is the emergence of a third power in Game Awards voting: Brazil, which has increased its footprint by four outlets and now commands 14 votes, just a whisker behind the British and Americans. This is part of a continuing surge in jury members from Latin American countries, which now make up around 21% of the jury.

Meanwhile, the Anglophone voting bloc of the U.S., U.K., Canada, and Australia is on the wane; the influence of East and Southeast Asia has dropped slightly (China has just three votes); and mainland Europe has consolidated the big increase in jury membership it made last year, now closely rivaling the English-language media by 27% to 28% of the jury, respectively.

Why did the number of American outlets on the jury drop so sharply? The story here is a mass exodus of mainstream, lifestyle, and tech media. Entertainment Weekly, Esquire, Inverse, Rolling Stone, The Atlantic, Wirecutter, and Wired have all left the jury. It's a very pronounced trend, although I couldn't tell you what's behind it. Perhaps it's a deliberate choice by The Game Awards; perhaps, in the current difficult media climate, these publications have lost their gaming writers.

Last year, I wrote about how an increasingly internationally diverse jury didn't necessarily mean a more diverse group of nominated games. In particular, representation for indie games has shrunk across the categories, likely a side-effect of the fact smaller studios can't often afford to have their games localized into many languages. As the jury has grown, its taste has shrunk, focusing on the kind of games that can travel easily all over the world.

I stand by this argument, but I'd like to note one caveat. There's one way, tallying perfectly with the changes in the jury, in which the games represented at The Game Awards are much more diverse than they used to be: country of origin.

At the Spike Video Game Awards, TGA's predecessor, the Game of the Year winner was far more likely to be an American game than not. Between 2014 and 2020, American games won GOTY at The Game Awards four times out of seven. But since then, there have been no American wins, with the GOTY award going to Sweden, Belgium, France, and Japan (twice). Glossy action-adventures have fallen away (in terms of GOTY wins, if not nominations), with the international jury seeming to prefer RPGs and family games like It Takes Two and Astro Bot.

Is the hegemony of the all-American AAA blockbuster in the GOTY race really over? Well, we'll see. You can't get more glossy than this year's overwhelming favorite, Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar Games is headquartered in New York. The game's subject is America. A good proportion of the thousands of people who have worked on it are American, in the San Diego and Los Angeles studios. The lead development studio for Grand Theft Auto games remains, as always, Rockstar North, in Edinburgh, Scotland — but at this point, maybe that's a technicality. Time for one last hurrah, then. But I await the first Brazilian GOTY winner with interest.

articles.headline: Trump tries different approach with Russia to bring Americans relief amid ongoing war with Ukraine
keyFacts: President Donald Trump temporarily eased restrictions on Russian diesel, arguing the move will lower global prices and encourage peace talks.
Bipartisan lawmakers and Ukrainian officials opposed the decision, arguing it benefits Russia while Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Treasury authorized Russian diesel transactions through April 2027 as lawmakers push to enforce a new sanctions law starting October 18.
body: President Donald Trump is easing some of the economic pressure on Russia in hopes of bringing Vladimir Putin closer to a peace deal — a gamble that will test whether economic incentives can move Moscow where years of sanctions have not.

The administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel has drawn opposition from Republicans on Capitol Hill and skepticism over whether the move will meaningfully lower prices for Americans.
Meanwhile, Russia has offered few public signs of concessions in return.

Six Republican senators joined Democrats this week in urging Trump to reverse the decision, while five House Republicans signed a separate bipartisan letter Thursday seeking to revoke the Treasury authorization.
The resistance comes as Washington approaches an Oct. 18, 2026, deadline to begin implementing a sweeping new sanctions law Congress overwhelmingly approved to increase economic pressure on Russia.
BIPARTISAN SENATORS DEMAND TRUMP SCRAP RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL, CALL IT 'BETRAYAL' OF US ALLIES

The administration argues that allowing Russian diesel back onto global markets could help bring down prices for American consumers while demonstrating the economic benefits Russia could gain through improved relations with the United States.

Trump has defended the agreement as a way to add supply to a global diesel market strained by high prices, stressing that the Russian fuel does not necessarily need to come state side to benefit American consumers.
"That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices," Trump told reporters Tuesday.

But energy analysts have questioned whether the volumes involved would meaningfully affect prices. Russia, meanwhile, continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire Sunday.

John Hardie, deputy director of the Russia Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, argued the diesel agreement would make more sense as part of a reciprocal deal under which Moscow and Kyiv both stopped attacking energy infrastructure.
"The Ukrainians could stomach it if it were part of a mutual energy truce where both Russia and Ukraine don't strike each other's infrastructure," Hardie told Fox News Digital.
Instead, Hardie said, Trump pressed Ukraine to halt its refinery strikes without securing the same restraint from Putin.
"The better solution is to go back to the Kremlin and try to get that two-way solution," he said.

Trump announced the diesel agreement Oct. 9 after a phone call with Putin, saying Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the "American and Global Marketplace," followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons shortly thereafter and eventually another 3 million tons depending on the condition of its refineries.
TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET'
Treasury issued General License 135 the same day, temporarily authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027.
The diesel dispute has become part of a broader strain between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has repeatedly pressed Kyiv to halt refinery attacks, while Zelenskyy has criticized the diesel deal and accused Russia of ignoring Trump's energy ceasefire. Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian oil infrastructure this week after saying Moscow had failed to observe the pause.

Russia, meanwhile, has intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy system as winter approaches. A major missile and drone attack Wednesday damaged dozens of energy facilities and left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power, according to Ukrainian officials.
The White House says the deal serves two purposes: adding supply to global fuel markets and showing Moscow some of the economic benefits that could come with improved relations.

Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the agreement with Ukrainian officials as part of an effort to revive peace negotiations, Reuters reported. One person briefed on the talks said the deal could help "soften" Moscow's position by signaling that Trump remains open to doing business with Russia.
But analysts question how much genuinely new diesel Russia can provide.
"The amount of diesel Russia can provide would be a drop in the bucket compared to global demand," Masha Kotkin, a fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told S&P Global.
"If you are asking about US diesel prices, I don't think it's going to make a difference," she said.

Sergey Vakulenko, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center and former Russian oil executive, similarly cautioned against treating the roughly $7 billion value of the diesel contemplated under the agreement as new revenue for Moscow, noting that Russia was already exporting substantial quantities despite Western sanctions.

He estimated the sanctions relief could instead benefit Russian exporters by roughly $30 to $40 per ton through better commercial terms and lower shipping costs — tens of millions of dollars per month, only part of which would reach the Russian state through taxes.

At the same time, Ukrainian strikes have sharply constrained Russia's ability to increase supply. Vakulenko said Russian diesel available for export fell from roughly 3 million tons per month in April to about 325,000 tons in September, leaving both Russia's additional financial benefit and the deal's potential impact on global prices more limited than the headline figures suggest.
Hardie said signs of division between Washington and Kyiv could encourage Putin to increase military pressure rather than compromise.
"That message of irresolution and of division between Washington and Kyiv only encourages Putin to intensify military pressure, kind of seeing that opportunity," Hardie said.

He said the administration had previously presented sanctions relief and renewed economic ties as benefits Russia could unlock through a negotiated settlement. Offering some of those benefits beforehand, he warned, could undermine that incentive.
"It'll lead Putin to kind of digging his heels in on maximalist demands," Hardie said.
The debate comes as Congress is moving in the opposite direction.

Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law Sept. 18, giving the administration new authorities to target Russian officials, financial institutions and entities helping sustain the war. Its first 30-day implementation deadline arrives Oct. 18.

Six Republican senators — Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski, Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn — joined six Democrats Tuesday in calling on Trump to rescind the diesel agreement and implement the new sanctions law.
The senators acknowledged the need to bring down energy costs but argued the Russian diesel would have a "negligible impact" on prices while generating additional revenue for Moscow.
A separate bipartisan group of 22 House lawmakers called on Trump Thursday to revoke the diesel authorization and fully implement the Graham law.
The White House has stood by the agreement, arguing Trump's priority is lowering costs for Americans while continuing to pursue an end to the war.
Hardie questioned whether economic incentives would carry enough weight to change Putin's calculations.

"Putin cares much more at this point about Ukraine and his legacy, and this broader kind of cocktail of grievances that led him to this war than he does about, you know, clearly Russia's GDP or well-being, or else he never would have done this in the first place," Hardie said.

The diesel agreement now puts Trump's theory of leverage to an early test: whether giving Putin a glimpse of the economic benefits available through improved relations can draw him toward a settlement, or whether Moscow will see easing pressure before a ceasefire as a reason to hold out for more.

articles.headline: Small business owners are doing OK – but will that help Trump overcome his low approval ratings?
keyFacts: Recent reports show small businesses are maintaining stable confidence and solid revenues ahead of the November midterm elections.
US small businesses employ half the nation's workforce and generate half its GDP, making them an influential voting bloc.
Small business sentiment remains generally optimistic despite challenges like inflation, which could affect Donald Trump's poor overall economic ratings.
body: There are 34m small businesses in the United States. They employ approximately half of the country’s workers and generate about half of the country’s GDP. They’re an important voting block. So how are they feeling about the economy as we head into November’s midterm elections? Overall, economic sentiment for Donald Trump is poor but small business – admittedly a diverse demographic that’s hard to poll – seems fairly confident. A number of recently published surveys and reports can help understand their mood.
Confidence is generally stable.

This week, the National Federation of Independent Businesses said that its Small Business Optimism Index fell to just below its long-term average, while uncertainty rose slightly. Labor quality was the top concern for 26% of owners and inflation for 20%. Expansion plans weakened, though 17% still plan to add jobs during the next three months.

However, small-business confidence improved significantly in the third quarter, according to the recently published Justworks/US Chamber Small Business Index. Some 72% of the 750 small businesses surveyed say they are comfortable with their current cash flow, but only 27% believe the US economy is in good health. Inflation remains the biggest problem, cited by 54% of owners.
Hiring is not strong, but not weak either.

HR platform Gusto estimated that small businesses added 28,000 jobs in September, making it the eighth consecutive month of employment gains following a decline in January. According to the company’s data, hiring accelerated from August’s revised gain of 18,500 jobs and growth was broad across industries, regions and company sizes, with healthcare and social assistance among the strongest sectors. Particularly notable is that some of the smallest employers continue to participate in the expansion, rather than job growth being concentrated solely among larger companies.

In its latest Small Business Employment Watch report, Paychex, another large HR and payroll processing service (and a client of my company), said that hiring in September essentially matched its 2026 year-to-date average with overall employment among companies with fewer than 50 employees appearing “stable”.

ADP, the country’s largest HR and payroll processing service, reported that US private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, with hiring accelerating for the first time since May following three months of slowing growth. Education and healthcare and leisure and hospitality led the gains, while financial activities and professional and business services were weaker. Importantly for small businesses, establishments employing one to 19 workers added 18,000 jobs. According to ADP, private-sector employers have not shifted into recession mode and although hiring has cooled from earlier periods, businesses are still adding employees.

Intuit painted a slightly different jobs picture. Its Intuit QuickBooks Small Business Index, which is based on data it gathers from its millions of QuickBooks customers, found that employment at US businesses with one to nine employees fell by 7,000 jobs in September and that jobs declined across most sectors and regions.
Revenues remain solid.

Intuit’s QuickBooks data shows that revenues moved sharply up this past month as inflation-adjusted average monthly revenue increased 1.68% and growth occurring in 11 of 12 industries, every region and 19 of 20 states.

Fiserv, a payment-processing service, said that its September data showed improving sales among US small businesses. However, the company reports that consumer behavior remains selective and that traffic has been weaker even as customers spend more when they do shop.
Economic growth continued in the third quarter.

Overall, US manufacturing remained firmly in expansion territory in September. The Institute for Supply Management’s Manufacturing Purchasing Manager’s Index marked its ninth consecutive month of growth after years of contraction. Despite rising prices, new orders, production and employment all remained expansionary and order backlogs increased. As usual, the ISM reported yet another month of expansion in the service sector (it’s been 27 consecutive months) with new orders remaining “particularly strong”.

The Wall Street Journal and other media sources reported recently that first-quarter annualized growth was revised to 2.5% from 2.1%, and second-quarter growth was increased to 2.2% from 1.5%, which, its editors argued, shows that the “US economy is performing considerably better than pessimistic headlines imply”.
Philadelphia lags in business creation.

My business is based in Philadelphia, a heavily Democratic area in a swing state. My clients appear to mostly be doing well so far this year but, like most small businesses around the country, continue to struggle navigating higher costs and a tight labor market.

This anecdotal evidence is somewhat supported by a May survey by WSFS Bank that found “surprisingly strong confidence among Philadelphia-area businesses” despite inflation and economic uncertainty. In that study, 92% of owners and business decision-makers say their companies are meeting or exceeding expectations, while 66% anticipate growth during the next year.

Philadelphia, however, has its own unique problems, particularly adding fewer small businesses per capita than other large cities. A recent study from Pew Research found that the number of Black-, Hispanic- and female-owned small businesses increased 39% between 2012 and 2022, showing meaningful entrepreneurial growth, but barriers including access to capital, regulatory requirements, taxes, commercial space and the difficulty of scaling companies continued to restrain business formation in the city.

The Democratic strategist James Carville once said that when it comes to electing candidates, “it’s the economy, stupid”. The good news for the Republicans is that the economy is resilient and the overall mood of the country’s small businesses is generally optimistic, despite the many challenges they face. But will that overcome the president’s low approval ratings?

articles.headline: Starfleet Academy: Where no progressive mind has gone before
keyFacts: Author Andrew Moore reviewed the television series Starfleet Academy in an article for the Washington Examiner.
Moore claimed that Starfleet Academy focuses on presenting progressive ideology rather than emphasizing meritocracy and adventure.
Moore stated that female characters disproportionately represent leadership, while male characters disproportionately serve as narrative adversaries.
body: Consider a glass of milk . It’s wholesome, nutritious, and quite satisfying. But try drinking an entire gallon in one sitting. The problem isn’t necessarily the milk. It’s the quantity and the insistence that you consume it all at once.

Each new Star Trek series fills me with anticipation that it will be as satisfying as the original. The premise of Starfleet Academy, of cadets progressing year by year, is fine. In fact, it offers considerable possibilities for adventure, rivalry, competition, personal growth, and the development of young people into competent Starfleet officers. I watched the entire season of Starfleet Academy and at some point, said to myself, “You’re Vulcan kidding me.” I was able to make it through the season largely because I’m a fanboy of Paul Giamatti.

The original Star Trek was progressive, particularly for its time. It challenged racial prejudice, explored social injustice, and imagined a future in which humanity had overcome many of its historical divisions. But it also gave us exploration, scientific curiosity, courage, duty, hierarchy, personal responsibility, and the occasional phaser fight. Its characters were expected to demonstrate competence, exercise judgment, and accept the consequences of their decisions. There was a sense of purpose and direction. There was meritocracy and a bit of humor from time to time. Kirk kissed Uhura. Fine, there is no issue there. Had Kirk kissed Sulu, George Takei’s famous “Oh my!” would have echoed across generations.
The original Star Trek could be progressive without making progressivism the protagonist.

Starfleet Academy, on the other hand, presents a rather different experience. Consider the distribution of authority and opposition. Women predominate among the identified teachers, occupy the three most prominent Academy and shipboard command roles, and provide much of the central institutional leadership. Men, meanwhile, predominate among the named characters who challenge Captain Ake through criminal activity, professional rivalry, diplomatic resistance, or personal hostility. They are, in fact, patriarchal foils utilized to promote a narrative, not a story. It may feel good to some progressives, but the illusion is tainted by the disproportion.

The issue isn’t that women command starships. That possibility was settled long ago, at least in the Star Trek universe. The more interesting observation is the apparent distribution of moral and institutional legitimacy. Women disproportionately represent enlightened leadership, while men disproportionately represent the attitudes, institutions, or threats that leadership must overcome. Even when male adversaries are rehabilitated, their narrative function has already served its purpose.
Any one of these choices might be unremarkable. Taken together, they begin to resemble a formula.
Then there is the gay Klingon, the lesbian alien relationship, the barefoot captain, and celebrity stunt-casting. Why not a transgender Klingon? Was that a bridge too far?

To be fair, some conservative viewers suffer from a sort of cultural lactose intolerance —reacting with immediate indigestion to the mere presence of diversity before a single line of dialogue is spoken. But before someone fires a phaser in my direction, let me emphasize that the existence of any one of these characters or relationships isn’t the problem. Nor must an identity-centered storyline interrupt the main plot to become noticeable. The issue is cumulative. At some point, the viewer begins recognizing the writers’ ideological choices more readily than the fictional world they are supposed to inhabit.

And what of meritocracy? The Academy ought to be a place where ability, discipline, competition, courage, and judgment are tested. Not everyone should be equally capable of commanding a starship simply because everyone deserves respect. Equality of human dignity and equality of competence are two very different propositions. Starfleet officers should earn their responsibilities, and the audience should see them do it. It was competency of each of the crews’ positions integrated with who they were as people that the original series exemplified.

In Starfleet Academy, those older concerns seem secondary to a different set of priorities. The result is less a sense of young officers preparing to meet an uncertain universe than a series anxious to reassure us of its own moral outlook. Which brings me back to the food analogy, and to something I would call Progressive Ideology Pornography.

Food porn isn’t simply a picture of food. It is food presented in a selectively intensified form, with exaggerated visual appeal, designed to stimulate rather than provide nourishment. Pornography , more generally, isolates and amplifies particular stimuli that produce a desired response. The experience is concentrated, immediate, and gratifying, while much of the complexity of ordinary human experience is stripped away.

PIP operates through a similar mechanism. Complex social realities are compressed into recognizable moral narratives. Virtue and victimhood are amplified, opponents are simplified, and expressions of ideological commitment become spectacles of moral affirmation. The viewer is invited to experience the satisfaction of recognizing the righteous position rather than being challenged to consider the full complexity of the issue.

The defining characteristic isn’t necessarily that the underlying progressive ideas are false. It’s that they are presented as an emotional product rather than propositions to be examined. Conservative, nationalist, and religious ideologies are equally capable of producing their own varieties of ideological pornography. No political persuasion enjoys a monopoly on self-gratification.

In Starfleet Academy, the issue is one of proportion and integration. PIP need not replace the storyline or interrupt an adventure to become conspicuous. It can operate through repeated choices about who exercises authority, who is morally credible, which relationships receive emphasis, and what qualities the narrative rewards. Individually, those choices may seem perfectly reasonable. Collectively, they can become predictable. In effect, the viewer is being asked to consume a gallon of milk each episode, and the viewer begins to expect it.

Once the viewer begins anticipating the ideological formula, the suspension of disbelief suffers. Instead of wondering what an unfamiliar civilization might be like, or how an inexperienced cadet might respond to danger, I find myself anticipating the next demonstration of the writers’ progressive sensibilities.

And that is where the pornography analogy becomes particularly relevant. The purpose of a story is to draw the audience into an imagined world. The purpose of an ideologically intensified presentation is to elicit a particular response. When the latter becomes too conspicuous, the audience may find itself responding to the stimulus rather than becoming absorbed in the story.

I wanted to watch cadets discover strange new worlds, confront difficult choices, and develop into officers worthy of the original series. Instead, I found myself increasingly aware of the people writing their adventures. Perhaps that’s the ultimate failure of proportion. The fictional universe becomes less interesting than the ideology being projected upon it.
A DEFTLY PLOTTED NEW NOVEL FROM RICHARD RUSSO
Star Trek once invited us to boldly go where no one had gone before. I would settle for a little more adventure and a little less assurance that the writers are on the right side of history.
Live long and prosper.
Andrew Moore is a small-business owner and author of the Primus Aeternus series.

articles.headline: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
keyFacts: Cities and states are enacting local regulations to restrict robotaxis because federal autonomous vehicle legislation remains stalled in Congress.
Municipal rules create a patchwork of operating, zoning, and emergency requirements that complicates deployments for robotaxi companies.
Autonomous vehicle developers are planning international expansions and prioritizing states that prevent individual cities from banning driverless technology.
body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
How it started

The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.

Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.

While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.

The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.
How it’s going

Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.

Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.

It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.

Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.

Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
What happens next

As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.

Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.

Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.
By the way

- Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.

- Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.
Read this
- Streetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York.
- Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports.
- Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan.

articles.headline: Startup makes tiny 'benchtop' fusion devices for more efficient reactors
keyFacts: Startup Cambridge Heavy Industries is developing a compact benchtop fusion device using two lasers, according to CEO Yun Kai.
The device is currently focused on producing tritium fuel rather than generating electricity, TechRadar reported.
The company aims to eventually scale the design into reactors roughly the size of two basketball courts, according to Kai.
body: Nuclear fusion is how stars (including our own Sun) create their energy, and scientists are hopeful it could one day be used as a clean, abundant energy solution here on Earth. There are no carbon emissions, most of the fuel required is widely available, and it's safe: if the reaction goes wrong, it simply peters out and stops.

You might have spotted the big challenge, which is trying to fit an entire star's worth of energy production inside a power plant. Two main approaches are being explored, one using magnets to create the incredibly high temperatures and pressures required, and one using lasers — which is where the startup Cambridge Heavy Industries comes in.

As TechCrunch reports, the company is currently operating in 'stealth mode' from a lab attached to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), but now seems ready to share some details about the technology it's developing. The main innovations: fusion that's more efficient and needs less room than conventional reactors.
Nuclear fusion on a tabletop

Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries, describes the company's fusion device as "tiny" and "benchtop" sized, which means experiments can be carried out and improved upon quickly. The technology will eventually be scaled up, but the aim is to build something smaller than conventional reactor designs — the size of two basketball courts approximately, rather than a full power plant complex.

What makes the approach of Cambridge Heavy Industries different is the dual laser setup. The first laser delivers its light as concentric rings that hit the block of fuel, designed to create shock waves traveling inward that create an accelerating compression effect; the second laser then hits the wave at the perfect spot to produce the super-high pressure required for ignition and nuclear fusion.

The enclosed system effectively acts as its own self-contained, compact fuel factory, because everything is moving inwards. It's also designed around a 2D rather than a 3D setup, which means fewer angles to cover — the laser fusion setup at the National Ignition Facility (NIF) in the US uses an array of 192 lasers in three dimensions to compress its own fuel blocks, for example.

As it's smaller and more efficient, the Cambridge Heavy Industries benchtop device can get through 50–80 laser shots per day — at the NIF, it's just a handful. A relatively low amount of laser power is required, says Kai, and as dozens of experiments are being done every 24 hours, the system can be quickly analyzed and iterated over time.

There is one big caveat: the tabletop device at Cambridge Heavy isn't doing the same job as the NIF reactor or any other reactor in development, not yet. For now, it's focused on making one of the fuels required for nuclear fusion, tritium, rather than generating electricity. The actual reactor and plant stages will come later.
What happens next

For nuclear fusion to happen, two light atoms need to be smashed together. The best combination, scientists think, will be deuterium and tritium — and while there's a lot of deuterium around, there's not much tritium at all. At the moment, most of what we have comes from older nuclear fission power plants that are being phased out.

The long-term plan is for nuclear reactors to make their own tritium alongside producing electricity, but with reactors not expected to come online until the 2030s at the earliest, there's a window of opportunity before then that Cambridge Heavy Industries is hoping to make the most of.

TechCrunch points to a recent study that suggests the tritium shortfall could be as much as 28 kilograms (62 pounds) for the industry as a whole by 2054. At today's prices that works out at around $840 million (£631 million / AU$1,209 million) worth of the isotope — a potentially lucrative market.

There's also a lot of money, potentially, in nuclear fusion in general, which is why investors are putting capital into the development of future fusion plants. It's worth bearing in mind that while nuclear fusion reactions have been produced in the lab for decades, we're not yet at the stage where they can practically produce electricity — that's still some years off.

A steady supply of tritium and more efficient, compact nuclear fusion reactors will certainly help us get there faster though, and that's what's driving Cambridge Heavy Industries. If the technology can be fully developed over the next few years, it promises to be a genuine game-changer for energy production and supply.

articles.headline: Tenebris Somnia Blends 2D Visuals With Live-Action Horror Scenes, And It’s Already On Sale At Launch
keyFacts: The horror game Tenebris Somnia blends retro two-dimensional pixel visuals with live-action cutscenes.
Andrés Borghi, Tobías Rusjan, and Saibot Studios co-created the title, which is published by New Blood Interactive.
Steam keys for Tenebris Somnia are currently on sale at Fanatical for $18.24 or £13.13 at launch.
body: Horror games live or die by their scares and tension. If the player isn’t uncomfortable guiding a character through dreadful situations, well, you may as well be playing an action-adventure game (don’t mention the first Uncharted’s final act, please). Tenebris Somnia blends the discomfort of retro horror with live-action sequences that will make your goosebumps bump, and you can get it cheaper than ever right now.

As the best horror games continue to push for more realistic visuals and immersive experiences, Tenebris Somnia’s twist on the genre combines old-school cool with movie-like cutscenes. It’s both jarring and original, and that’s exactly what makes for excellent horror. I want to be constantly surprised, and Tenebris Somnia makes its pixelated 2D threats even more menacing when you see live-action versions of the monsters.

Inspired by classics that scared us silly, like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, Tenebris Somnia has a deceptively simple premise. You play as Julia, who finds herself in a parallel universe while visiting her ex-boyfriend and is relentlessly hunted by nightmares that, well, aren’t exactly figments of her imagination. (To be honest, visiting an ex sounds like a nightmarish experience on its own. Ba-dum, tsss.)
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A_fQ_gNddbo

Co-created by Andrés Borghi and Tobías Rusjan with Saibot Studios, and published by New Blood Interactive, the studio behind Ultrakill, Blood West, and Gloomwood, Tenebris Somnia’s style is fittingly inspired by past eras of console gaming. Its pixelated visuals make the switch to live-action cutscenes even more unsettling. It’s almost like Clock Tower, but if it randomly turned into a movie at any second. No, I’m not shaking; you are .

If you’re looking to rewind to those retro vibes while adding something new to your scary movie marathon this spooky season, you can grab a Steam key for Tenebris Somnia for just $18.24 / £13.13 at Fanatical . That makes it a tempting way to experience a brand-new and genuinely unusual horror game for less. Not bad, unless, of course, you don’t like losing sleep.

articles.headline: Outlast designer says that one playtester was so upset by the horror series they 'ran out of the studio to go cry outside' and didn't return
keyFacts: Red Barrels co-founder Philippe Morin said an Outlast playtester once ran outside crying and never returned due to the graphic content.
Morin stated Red Barrels warns job applicants during interviews about the studio's graphic content and required discussions.
PC Gamer reported that Red Barrels is unlikely to soften its graphic approach if it ever creates Outlast 3.
body: Red Barrels' Outlast series has long held a reputation for pushing the envelope further than most horror games, with depictions of violence, gore and nudity that can be shocking even within a medium well versed in delivering scares. But it isn't just audiences who have found the studio's games shocking beyond the virtual horror norm. As co-founder Phillipe Morin recently revealed, there have been numerous instances where people in and around the studio have found working with the material frightening to the point of being traumatic.

In a chat with Gamespot, Morin discussed the studio's unflinching approach to horror, explaining that it wasn't a deliberate attempt to court controversy, and was simply a "personal preference" on Morin and the other co-founders' behalf. "We didn't start like 'Oh, we've got to make the goriest game out there'" Morin explained. "It was just, 'we're making a horror game, so obviously we'll make it gory. I remember even the scriptwriter early on was saying, 'There's never too much blood.'"

Nonetheless, the intense and graphic nature of Outlast' horror has proved triggering within the studio. During the interview, Morin recalls one incident involving an individual associated with Red Barrels—possibly an employee, though Morin doesn't state this explicitly. "We started pushing and pushing, and you know, I remember there was a playtest, and somebody, after a couple of hours, basically ran out of the studio to go cry outside." Apparently, this person never returned to the studio.

Morin says that Red Barrels is not oblivious to the potential effect of its games on people, and that this informs how the studio approaches recruitment. "When we do job interviews, we always make sure that people are fully aware of the kind of content we create and the kind of conversations needed to create that content," he explains, adding that "People have to be comfortable with that because obviously you hear stuff in the studio that [if] you said the same thing in a different studio, you'd end up in a meeting with HR."

Yet these attempts at transparency with potential employees have not always been successful, as Morin explains. "We had one case of somebody who started working with us on Monday, and then on Thursday they resigned because even though they knew about the gore and the violence, they had a blind spot for other things, more so about religion, and they were not comfortable with that." While Morin doesn't specify when this occurred, it's likely that it happened during the development of Outlast 2, the story of which revolves around a violent Christian cult.

Yet while some people may have found Red Barrels' horror to be too much, the broader audience has absolutely lapped it up. The most recent game in the series, The Outlast Trials, sold half a million copies in its first week of early access, while the series as a whole has attracted a whopping 60 million players since 2013. Hence, if Red Barrels ever does make Outlast 3, it's unlikely the studio will soften its approach.
