articles.headline: House panel warns Singham-linked nonprofits: Comply with subpoenas or face Congress
keyFacts: The House Ways and Means Committee warned three Singham-linked nonprofits to comply with document subpoenas by Tuesday, lawmakers announced.
Lawmakers are investigating whether millions of dollars from Neville Roy Singham's nonprofit network advanced Chinese Communist Party interests in the United States.
Leaders of the three groups and Singham could face congressional questioning under oath if they fail to comply with the deadline.
body: Lawmakers have escalated their probe of three nonprofits linked to Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham's funding network, warning that their leaders — and even Singham himself — could be hauled before Congress to answer questions under oath unless they comply with subpoenas by Tuesday.

In new letters announced this week, the Republican-led House Ways and Means Committee renewed its demands for financial records and other documents as lawmakers investigate whether millions of dollars flowing through Singham's network of tax-exempt nonprofits are being used to advance Chinese Communist Party interests in the United States.

Singham himself is among 21 individuals identified by the committee for potential questioning under oath, according to Fox News Digital sources. The list includes nonprofit executives, activists and journalists associated with the three organizations.
PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS
DOJ LAUNCHES GRAND JURY PROBE INTO MARXIST MOGUL NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S FUNDING OF LEFTIST GROUPS

The letters were sent to The People's Forum Inc., a New York City-based activist hub; BreakThrough News, a left-wing nonprofit media outlet that shares a Manhattan address with The People's Forum; and Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research, a Massachusetts-based Marxist think tank.

"Shanghai Singham has poured millions of dollars into these groups to take advantage of America's nonprofit sector and promote Chinese Communist Party propaganda. That much is public. What these groups are fighting to keep hidden is even more concerning," Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., said in a statement .
"Either these organizations turn over the documents, or their leaders will answer the Committee's questions under oath."
The threatened depositions mark another escalation in a dispute that began with requests for financial records in 2025 and intensified when the committee subpoenaed the three nonprofits in July.
The organizations have challenged the investigation , arguing lawmakers are targeting their political views and First Amendment-protected activities.
The potential deposition targets include eight individuals at The People's Forum, seven at BreakThrough News and six at Tricontinental.

Among those named are The People's Forum executive director Manolo De Los Santos, education director Layan Fuleihan and organizing director David Chung; BreakThrough News editor-in-chief Ben Becker, news director Zoe Alexandra and chief correspondent Rania Khalek; and Tricontinental executive director Vijay Prashad and Singham, who is listed as chairman of its international advisory board.
The committee has not publicly announced that deposition subpoenas have been issued to any of the individuals.
SUBPOENAED PRO-CHINA OUTLET DEFENDS ITSELF ON DEMOCRACY NOW!, WHICH PAID SINGHAM-FOUNDED COMPANY MILLIONS

The panel alleges that Singham channeled money through shell companies and donor-advised funds before it reached the three tax-exempt groups. Such arrangements, the committee said, can allow foreign-linked funding to pass through intermediaries that "by design, obscure the original source of the contribution."
Singham is an American-born technology tycoon and longtime Marxist activist who sold his software company, ThoughtWorks, for an estimated $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai.

Fox News Digital previously traced at least $278 million from Singham into six core U.S. nonprofits that served as funding hubs within a broader international network of activist groups, media organizations and think tanks promoting socialist, communist and pro-China causes.

Of that funding, the investigation found $22.44 million flowed to The People's Forum, $16.76 million to Tricontinental and $1.098 million to BreakThrough BT Media Inc., the parent organization of BreakThrough News. Together, the three received approximately $40.3 million, according to the investigation, which the committee cited in its earlier correspondence.
The committee says it is examining whether existing tax laws adequately protect against foreign influence in the nonprofit sector and whether Congress should strengthen those laws.

Separately, Singham is under federal grand jury investigation in the Southern District of New York over alleged financial crimes involving his nonprofit funding network, as previously reported by Fox News Digital. The investigation is examining possible wire fraud, bank fraud, money laundering and other financial offenses. No criminal charges against Singham have been announced.

BreakThrough News condemned the latest demands in an Oct. 9 statement on its website, accusing the committee of targeting its journalists because of their political views. The outlet said it receives no outside editorial direction and that its major donations come from U.S. organizations.
During an episode of its BT Live program, hosts Alexandra and Khalek, both named among those facing potential depositions, denounced the committee's demands.
"Unless BT gives up its legal rights, including our First Amendment protections, he'll subpoena each of us individually and drag us to Washington for depositions," Alexandra said.
Khalek accused lawmakers of targeting journalists personally after the outlet challenged earlier demands.
"They will come after us individually if we don't comply with their unconstitutional demands," she said.
BreakThrough News also urged supporters to sign a petition opposing the investigation and donate to help cover its legal expenses.
Fox News Digital contacted all three organizations and their attorneys for comment on the latest demands but had not received a response as of publication.

The investigation has also drawn accusations of McCarthyism from prominent left-wing figures, including Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who called the July subpoenas "the McCarthy trials" and warned, "They will come for you," and CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, who described them as a "terrible attack on independent journalism."
‘MCCARTHY TRIALS’: HASAN PIKER, FAR-LEFT FIGURES ERUPT OVER SUBPOENAS IN $39M SINGHAM PROBE

The committee first sought records from The People's Forum in September 2025 and expanded its investigation to BreakThrough News and Tricontinental in February 2026. After the organizations challenged the requests, lawmakers narrowed their demands in May before issuing subpoenas in July.
The committee sought records involving foreign-linked funding, financial arrangements, communications with Singham and other foreign interests, and information about donors and overseas grants.

Attorneys for BreakThrough News and The People's Forum formally objected in August, arguing the subpoenas violated First Amendment protections and demanded information beyond the committee's legitimate legislative authority.

"A witch-hunt is not a valid legislative purpose," the attorneys wrote in their Aug. 7 responses, comparing the investigation to the House Un-American Activities Committee's investigations of suspected communist influence during the 1940s and 1950s.

The organizations also accused lawmakers of repeatedly changing the stated purpose of the investigation as they challenged earlier requests. Both left open the possibility of responding if the committee narrowed or revised its demands.
The committee rejected those arguments, maintaining that its investigation concerns the organizations' finances and structure rather than their political views or journalism.

articles.headline: The Sunday Papers
keyFacts: Rock Paper Shotgun published a digest highlighting commentary on Palestinian identity, war films, horror storytelling, transgender rights, and artificial intelligence.
NHS England banned transgender women from female-only hospital wards, which the author stated limits healthcare access and strains resources.
Arundhati Roy reported that India is approving massive artificial intelligence data centres with virtually zero environmental oversight.
body: Sundays are for firing up Twine again and thinking you know what, if this swanky IF plotter had been around when I was an undergraduate, I might have preserved all my exam revision notes in text adventure form. I still have two, reassuringly heavy boxes of tabbed and colour-coded index cards that you could plausibly lay out to form a maze, navigable by compass commands. Head down the western corridor from Middle English to the Renaissance, and – ah, bollocks, you have been eaten by a Grue. Surely somebody's thought of this, in the decade and change since Twine was released? I mean, we already have 3D museum exhibits extracted from Wikipedia.

Sundays are also for heading to the allotment and getting annoyed with the tomato plants, who have decided to go bonkers right at the end of the growing season. I thought you were done, pesky nightshades. I thought I could leave you alone for the rest of the year. Finally, Sundays are for sharing good criticism, like the below.
Here's a hard and hopeful essay from Palestinian writer and academic Dana El Kurd about different kinds of silence, following the revelation that she has a Jewish Israeli great-grandmother.

Rachel’s story provoked many questions. I wondered if I had lost relatives in the Holocaust. I must have—Rachel’s family was still in Poland in 1935. I wondered, if there were survivors, whether they ended up in Israel. They surely served in the army, if so. Did they kill any Palestinians? Did they end up in Gaza?

Right now, I would rather not know the answers to these questions, not as I continue to watch a genocide unfold. I doubt Rachel’s descendants want anything to do with me either. She concealed the identities of her Israeli children in the interview, saying there were “sensitivities” around the issue. Clearly their background is a secret they keep to themselves as well.

How might Rachel’s life have looked had it not been overtaken by the Israeli state-building project? Her story speaks to thornier issues that Palestinians grapple with constantly in their struggle for self-determination. What do you do when your colonizer has no home country to return to? How did my grandfather, a devout Palestinian man, make peace with his Israeli mother, and what might this say about coexistence? Is there some way to reform Israeli society, twisted by ethnonationalism though it is?

For the London Review of Books blog, Iza Ding compares Wen Muye's film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East to Hollywood's recreations of US wars in Iraq, identifying a different strain of interventionist mythmaking.

Chinese state media praised Once Upon a Time in the Middle East as a new kind of anti-war film, comparing it to All Quiet on the Western Front and Schindler’s List. The criticism of the US invasion is unsparing (there are plenty of lines like ‘You Americans think everyone is a terrorist’) but most of the individual American characters are humanised. Tony Wang (Aarif Lee), a Chinese American soldier from California, acts tough until, after a few shots of whiskey, all he can say is that he wants to go home. The Iraqis begin as innocent victims, but the film shows the ways in which ordinary, decent people can be gradually bent towards extremism by unbearable circumstances. The moral ambiguity is characteristic of Wen Muye. There are good guys – the Chinese – but no bad guys: the Americans are homesick and frightened; the Iraqis are grieving and enraged.

While we're at the cinema, here's John WM Thompson on Mike Flanagan's adaptation of Carrie and the bowdlerization of horror, with a few notes on the "cosy horror" that has crept into videogames of late.

Here in America, it is the market actors, not the people, who truly cannot abide tragic storytelling, resisting as it does linear franchising, four-quadrant reboots, children’s toy merchandising, so on and so forth. I believe that regular people, if you pushed them, would appreciate and embrace tragic storytelling — no one actually wants to eat candy all day every day, and few people are actually satisfied with endless pandering. But if they only see comedy, they will come only to expect comedy. If they are told that art must make them feel good and reflect an optimistic world, they will become dismayed and confused when offered the sour or bitter, enriching as they might be. They may seek to escape tragedy. And thus we would see depictions of complexity, complication, reality at its least friendly, all feared and reviled. It is already happening. By Flanagan’s own words, Carrie is part of that action.

NHS England has banned trans women from female-only hospital wards, the latest stroke in a campaign of institutional cruelty that will make it harder for trans people to access healthcare, while also increasing the burden on facilities who are strapped for space and resources. While reading around about this, I came across this essay on "why trans people deserve to be boring" from Ash Lazarus Orr - the named plaintiff in a federal lawsuit over the Trump administration’s passport policy for trans people in the US.

Marginalized people are often easiest to defend when we are sympathetic, and there is something deeply unfair about requiring someone to be likeable before deciding they are worthy of dignity. The trans person whose story is supposed to change someone’s mind is asked to be vulnerable enough to create empathy but composed enough to remain credible, angry enough that the harm feels real but not so angry that someone stops listening. After years of preparing for interviews and thinking about how something would land with an audience, I became very familiar with those calculations.

Sometimes those calculations are necessary. They are also exhausting when you realize how much freedom there is in being allowed to disappoint people only as yourself. A cisgender person can be an asshole without anyone treating their behavior as meaningful evidence about cisgender people as a population. Trans people deserve the same freedom to be mediocre, annoying, wrong or unlikeable without someone deciding our individual failures reveal something larger about whether people like us deserve to exist comfortably in the world.

For Equator, Arundhati Roy goes long about the North American tech billionaire class and generative AI, with a focus on self-serving industry calls for regulation and the ramifications for Indian workers in particular. We publish or share a lot of apocalyptic pieces about generative AI on these pages, and there's always a risk of wallowing in misery while generating nega-publicity for the chatbot tycoons, but Roy is a great rhetorician and this essay covers a lot of ground.

In her incisive, dagger-sharp book, Empire of AI, Karen Hao describes the ongoing, all-out plunder of land and resources, and the dragooning of workers in poor countries labouring on starvation wages to become “data capturers” to keep Cyclopes’ dreams afloat. Since there is unlikely to be enough water or electricity to feed the massive energy appetite of its companies and its $100 billion supercomputers, Cyclopes is aggressively lobbying for private nuclear plants and the rollback of safety protocols. As backup, billions of dollars are being poured into developing nonperishable sources of fusion energy, so that data centres can be moved into outer space or onto the moon.

Meanwhile, on dear, shabby old Earth, the government of India has stepped up to welcome the setting up of more energy-guzzling data centres. Six in Visakhapatnam alone, including a $15 billion hub for Google. They are being given clearance with virtually zero environmental oversight, as though they’re just buildings, warehouses. It’s an old tradition between India and the US – give us your garbage, your toxic industries, your poisoned chalice. We’ll treasure it. And as in the US, activists in India are putting their bodies on the line to stop the poisoning of the water and the air for the tens of thousands of people who live in the vicinity of the proposed “warehouses”.

Music this week is Gordon Lightfoot's Sundown, which appears in the OST for kind-of-alright Jawsalike miniseries Below. Have a lovely weekend, wherever you are. Please share any really interesting Twine games and bulk-cook tomato recipes you've discovered.

articles.headline: After Dubois' dominant win, what's next for heavyweight boxing?
keyFacts: Daniel Dubois retained his heavyweight title by stopping Fabio Wardley in two rounds at London's O2 Arena.
Filip Hrgovic wants a rematch with Dubois, while Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are scheduled to fight in December.
Promoter Frank Warren said he will work on staging a unification fight for Dubois next year.
body: - Published
Daniel Dubois' demolition of Fabio Wardley has strengthened his position among the heavyweight elite.
The 29-year-old needed only two rounds to stop his British rival at London's O2 Arena, retaining his title with a performance far more emphatic than their thrilling first encounter in May.
Dubois can now turn his attention towards unification and some of boxing's biggest names.
Meanwhile, Oleksandr Usyk is approaching retirement, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to meet and a new group of world champions are looking to establish themselves.
So what is next for the heavyweight division?
Who is next for Dubois - and where does Wardley go?
IBF champion Filip Hrgovic made his intentions clear, entering the ring after Dubois' victory, with both keen on a rematch.
Dubois stopped the Croatian in June 2024, but Hrgovic has since rebuilt his reputation, claiming the vacant IBF title with victory over British prospect Moses Itauma in August.
But Hrgovic, 34, has Cuba's Frank Sanchez waiting as a mandatory challenger.
Promoter Frank Warren is working towards staging Hrgovic's first defence in Croatia early next year, potentially delaying a reunion with Dubois.
The biggest financial prize for Dubois could be a meeting with the winner of Fury and Joshua's December showdown.
"All those names are there to do a unification fight next year and that's what we'll be working on," Warren said.
Wardley, meanwhile, has shown he can compete at world level, but the manner of Saturday's defeat exposed a gulf in technical ability.
A return against a lower-ranked opponent could help restore confidence, but questions remain over whether Wardley can make the adjustments needed to challenge the division's elite again.
Fury v Joshua - finally, but what happens afterwards?

After years of negotiations and false starts, Fury and Joshua are finally scheduled to meet at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on a card that begins on 11 December, with the main event expected in the early hours of 12 December.
The Netflix-streamed contest has demonstrated its extraordinary commercial appeal, with about 80,000 tickets selling out within an hour.
Warren says the vacant WBA 'super' title will be at stake, potentially opening the door to unification fights in 2027.
However, WBA 'regular' champion Murat Gassiev has questioned the decision and called for the winner to face him.
That appears unlikely to be a priority for either Briton, with both reportedly set to earn close to $100m (Â£75m) in December.
A rematch would offer another enormous payday, particularly if the first encounter is close or controversial, but a one-sided defeat could push the loser towards retirement.
Is Kabayel the forgotten champion?
Germany's Agit Kabayel has built one of the strongest records in the division.
The unbeaten 34-year-old has stopped Arslanbek Makhmudov, Sanchez and Zhilei Zhang, but remains a relatively unfamiliar name to casual boxing fans.
Kabayel, elevated to WBC champion when Usyk vacated, makes his first defence against Albania's Nelson Hysa on 28 November.
A unification fight against Dubois in 2027 could provide the opportunity to become a much bigger name in the sport.
Usyk's final fight - and what about Verhoeven and Wilder?
Usyk's decision to vacate the WBA, WBC and IBF titles in June means the unbeaten Ukrainian can call the shots over the final chapter of his career.
The pound-for-pound star, who defeated former kickboxing world champion Rico Verhoeven in May, has indicated he wants one final contest before retirement.
Dutchman Verhoeven exceeded expectations before suffering a controversial 11th-round stoppage defeat, and wants a rematch.
Verhoeven says he has accepted an offer to face Deontay Wilder on the Fury-Joshua undercard, although the American has yet to agree and has also been linked with cruiserweight Jai Opetaia.
Wilder previously emerged as a contender for Usyk's farewell, but negotiations appear to have stalled.
A third meeting between Usyk and Fury has also been mooted.
But having already beaten Fury, Joshua and Dubois twice apiece, how much more does Usyk have to prove?
How does Itauma rebuild?
Itauma's charge towards a world title was halted when he suffered his first professional defeat against Hrgovic.
Itauma, 21, is expected to return in January, with Warren promising credible opposition rather than a straightforward confidence-building contest.
The priority will be developing the stamina, pacing and tactical patience required over 12 rounds before pursuing another world title opportunity.
A rematch with Hrgovic remains a longer-term possibility, but there is little need to rush with time firmly on Itauma's side.
What else is happening on the global and domestic scene?
American Jarrell Miller remains highly ranked, while compatriots Jared Anderson and Richard Torrez Jr, an Olympic silver medallist, are rebuilding.
New Zealand's former world champion Joseph Parker is seeking a return after his provisional doping suspension was lifted in August.

Australia's Teremoana Teremoana has stopped all 12 professional opponents within two rounds, while Uzbekistan's two-time Olympic champion Bakhodir Jalolov extended his unbeaten record by beating Solomon Dacres on Saturday.
In Britain, Derek Chisora, 42, is considering another comeback and says he expects to face WBA 'regular' champion Gassiev in December.

British champion Richard Riakporhe is pursuing world honours after moving up from cruiserweight, while former cruiserweight world champion Lawrence Okolie is targeting a return after reaching an agreement with the WBC over an adverse drugs test finding.
David Adeleye, Dave Allen, Johnny Fisher and Frazer Clarke remain on the domestic scene, while Leo Atang, 19, and Ireland's Adam Olaniyan, 20, are emerging talents.
With Usyk, Fury and Joshua approaching the ends of their careers, the heavyweight division is entering a new era.
There is no shortage of potential big fights, but bringing the champions together before mandatory obligations, rematches and boxing politics get in the way could prove the greatest challenge.

articles.headline: Voicemod’s New Phone Gadget Changes Your ‘Sonic Identity’ for Mobile Games and Streaming
keyFacts: Voicemod opened preorders for the Key Pocket, a $130 magnetic phone soundboard that lets users alter their voices.
The device processes audio locally to provide privacy, accessibility, and personal expression for gamers and streamers, Voicemod representatives said.
Voicemod aims to eventually integrate its voice technology directly at the system level to eliminate the need for hardware, executives said.
body: For years, Voicemod has given people a way to change their voices online, which they’ve done for any number of benign reasons — for game players with feminine-pitched voices to avoid harassment, for those with damaged vocal cords to simulate their former voices, for anonymity or even just for fun. Now the company has a new product to bring its voice-changing tech on the go in a physical device that magnetically clips on the back of phones.

The Voicemod Key Pocket, available to preorder now for $130, is a small soundboard about the size of a magnetic battery and serves as a controller interface for the company’s voice-changing apps. The half-dozen buttons on the back of the device can be used to switch between voices or audio effects while streaming or playing games, while the wheel adjusts volume of the projected voice.

The Key Pocket works in tandem with the Voicemod app, but all voice processing is done locally and in real time separate from games and streaming apps in order to maximize privacy as well as performance, according to a Voicemod statement. The Voicemod app provides access to over 200 original voices made by the company, over 76,000 voices made by the service’s community and over 800,000 sounds and memes made by users.
More from CNET

The Key Pocket is a versatile gizmo, with an LED wheel at the top-left corner for toggling voices and checking sound setup, while programmable trigger buttons enable swapping between voices and soundboard playback. The device supports wired and Bluetooth wireless headsets, has USB passthrough charging and clips securely to the back of phones with MagSafe-compatible magnets.

Beyond phones, the Key Pocket works on tablets and consoles, including PS4 and PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2 and the Meta Quest 2, 3 and 3S headsets. It can plug into USB-C, wired 3.5mm ports or connect via Bluetooth.

There are plenty of reasons folks might want to change their voice, from goofing off with friends to avoiding harassment when gaming online — a sad reality for gamers with feminine voices. It’s also an accessibility boon for people who have health conditions or other circumstances leading them to want to change their vocal timbre and pitch.

These days, changing voices can be cause for concern, especially with artificial-intelligence scams spoofing the voices of loved ones to extort money. But when I sat down at Mobile World Congress 2026 earlier this year to chat with Voicemod’s Daniel Pearson, vice president of marketing, and Alex Bordanova, chief product and technology officer, they explained how it aligned with the ethos of the company. The Key Pocket is the result of years of Voicemod’s work to support the idea that one’s online voice is as much an expression of identity as their visual look.

“Everyone has their digital visual appearance where they tweak their cosmetics and skins, but when it comes to voice, it’s kind of been left out, right? It’s this missing half of digital identity,” said Pearson.

As voice-changing tech makes its way into Fortnite, Arc Raiders, Marvel Rivals and other spaces for online third spaces, people are opening up to the idea that their personal expression isn’t just limited to how they’re seen, but also how they’re heard — or as Pearson calls it, their “sonic identity.”
When voice becomes a way to express identity

In our earlier chat, Pearson and Bordanova laid out what Voicemod meant to its community, with the latter describing one memorable story from last October’s TwitchCon 2025. A woman approached him explaining that she was a streamer who lost her voice for about six months but was able to make up for it with Voicemod’s tech.
“She used an AI voice, because that was enough to turn something audible out of just very nuanced sounds that she could project,” Bordanova said.
It spurred discussion about ways the Voicemod team might preserve the community’s voices — a vault, say, to future-proof their voices in the event that health or injury might limit their speaking.

The Voicemod creators don’t just see its tech as just to alter voices for fun or privacy — they see it as an expression machine, one that reflects who you are online. That comes in the form of a voice tweaked to a desired pitch and timbre, but also more abstract communication, like a soundboard. Yes, the signature toy of radio shock jocks from yesteryear is an aspect of expression, too, especially among a community where sounds take on specific meanings.
“It’s giving you the capacity to react and expand by giving extra context that you and your friends understand, but the normies don’t,” said Pearson.

Voicemod’s team has been encouraged by the increasing availability of voice-changing tech in games. Around a year ago, Arc Raiders launched its voice changer in beta but only offered ten voices at launch, and Voicemod offered their own tech to expand those options.

“[Gamers] are social beings, they don’t want to have the default skin. They want to have their own skin customized,” Pearson said. “If the game just gives you 5-10 skins, you’re gonna want the next one, you want to differentiate yourself.”

The company’s Voicelab enables further voice tweaking with fun effects. One could, if they wanted, change their voice to sound like they were wearing a helmet in a cave inside a volcano — wacky but evocative sonic context placing the person in a specific space and circumstance. It enhances expression and storytelling and uses AI to do it. But not the AI you’re thinking of.
AI has been at the heart of Voicemod — but not generative AI

There’s no denying that technological advancement has enabled voice generation, but Voicemod came long before that. It was founded 14 years ago, using digital sound processing to alter voices, launching first on an iPhone 3GS, Bordanova explained.

What their tech enabled that traditional DSP could not is changing the timbre of the voice — its tone, color and personality. Using math, Voicemod’s tech could change a vocal signal in ways that would simulate changing the human organs that naturally shape one’s voice, like elongating or shrinking the vocal cords or altering the width of your throat or nose.

More traditional AI powered Voicemod’s older methods of voice changing, which improved thanks to technological developments. The company’s advantage was to be one of the first to invest heavily in AI’s use in voice changing, Bordanova said.
“There was something unique, something very special, that would evolve us from being a voice changer to having fun with friends online, into giving real utility for a 24/7 use case,” Bordanova said.

What he clarifies is that Voicemod’s tech isn’t based on generative AI, unlike the tech behind voice processing tricks like Google’s live translation. Instead, their language models are around 20 megabytes in weight, and take about a week to train. Unlike the immense large language models used in generative AI, Voicemod’s are small enough to fully download on phones and other client-side devices. They can be consulted immediately on device for 42 millisecond latency, rather than need to go to the cloud.

That doesn’t mean they’ll never use LLMs — but the use case they’re envisioning is as a glorified assistant helping people find the right toggles and settings to get the voice they want from existing choices.
“You can type, I want the voice of SpongeBob and the LLM would pick the right effect and parameters and just create the voice for us,” Bordanova said.
Expression on the go, through your phone to your digital life

Back in March at MWC 2026, I chatted with Bordanova and Pearson when they brought out a prototype for the Key Pocket, the follow-up to the company’s earlier Voicemod Key, a dongle device that aimed to help change voices for console play. Even in its cruder form, the Key Pocket felt special.

As even the prototype was MagSafe compatible, I clipped it to the back of my own iPhone 15 Pro Max. Even if the device wasn’t far enough along to be usable with software, I could still simulate how it would feel in action with my phone rotated sideways, as if I had it active while gaming. The row of buttons rested below my fingers, easy to press if I wanted to tweak my voice or trigger vocal or sound effects. The volume wheel was nice and accessible. If I was streaming or chatting with my friends, the Key Pocket would be a nice accessory to have.

While a lot of gaming happens at home on PC and console, mobile gaming is a huge sector. The Key Pocket is a neat tool for gamers who either play on the go or who opt to play on phones for other reasons — possibly because they can’t afford pricey bigger platforms, which have only gotten more expensive since the RAM shortage. Odds are good that the phone in many gamers’ pockets can play the games they want, and the Key Pocket could help with their so-called sonic identity.

Voicemod’s goal goes beyond the Key Pocket to eventually integrate their tech at a system level, so that anyone booting up a computer or phone could use the tens of thousands of voices created by the Voicemod community (along with the filters and sound effects) to modify their aural appearance anywhere on the device.
“The last frontier is to get rid of the hardware,” Bordanova said.

Expanding Voicemod’s tech across a device’s software and apps would broaden its appeal — imagine not just customizing your voice in games and voice chats with friends, but work Zooms and other calls. Having the same options and interface available everywhere you could use your voice would open up possibilities for folks who’ve never thought about tweaking their voices.

But any mobile gamer will tell you that external controls make a world of difference compared to on-screen digital buttons. Integrating voice tech into the back end of devices is good, but having the Key Pocket soundboard at the touch of your fingers is a far more tactile and responsive set of controls. For streamers and presenters on the go who rely on exact timing, the Key Pocket is a neat solution. Sometimes all you need is an attractively designed gadget to expose folks to new tech possibilities — and in this case, the potential to express themselves online in a way they may not have considered before.

articles.headline: In the age of AI, one man spent years squeezing an entire museum onto a Game Boy - Why? For the most human of reasons
keyFacts: Dr Marcel Pflug created a Game Boy cartridge and downloadable ROM containing a searchable reference museum about the handheld console.
Pflug said he spent years building the project to keep historical knowledge preserved directly on the original 1989 hardware.
Pflug plans to update the cartridge archive annually and is currently developing a Game Boy diagnostic tool called GB Test Lab.
body: "Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this. The world has many needs, and a Game Boy cartridge with no game inside it was not high on the list." So begins Dr Marcel Pflug's explanation for one of the most unexpected projects I've come across in a while: a Game Boy reference museum that isn't just a Game Boy reference museum; it's one that works on a Game Boy cartridge.

"I run this museum, a project that catalogues everything around the little grey machine," Pflug writes on the Game Boy Museum website, "and one day a thought took hold that I could not shake, mostly because it made me laugh. Every object in the collection is a museum piece, so what if the museum itself became one of them? A cartridge that plays nothing, that you slot into a real Game Boy, and that turns the machine into a guide to its own world. An exhibit about the collection, living inside the collection."

The Game Boy Museum, in its original website form, features a museum's worth of knowledge and exhibitions focusing on Nintendo's classic handheld. There's a dizzying array of Game Boy product shots, all neatly presented and organised; there's an entire archive of peripherals, including things as incidental as cables; there's a guide charting every micro-adjustment to the Game Boy's hardware over the ages; and there's a journal area collating hundreds of articles about the handheld. There is, in other words, a lot.

As comprehensive as it is, though, presenting it all online to browse using modern computers and devices is relatively straightforward. But cramming that onto a cartridge for a device made in 1989 is an entirely different matter. So there were immediate obstacles for Pflug's project. The Game Boy, Pflug discovered, is "a spectacularly bad e-reader", due to the limited 255 "blocks" it can show on screen. That's not a lot when you consider several blocks are used for every letter of text, and the museum is primarily a text-based affair. "Reading a museum on a Game Boy, it turns out, is a game of inches," Pflug notes.

He also wanted the Museum to display QR codes, as a way to point people towards photographs he couldn't show on the Game Boy, feeling there'd be something "quietly wonderful" about getting a piece of tech from the 80s to talk to a phone from the 2020s. But, of course, QR codes were never meant to be displayed on a Game Boy. As Pflug explains, they were created in 1994, well after the handheld's release, "to track parts on a Japanese car-factory floor". It was Toyota's factory, if you're wondering (that's your quiz bonus point).

Similar bespoke solutions were needed for things like displaying an image of Pflug in the credits, because apparently you can't simply convert a photo into the tones of a Game Boy screen. "The face becomes one pale blob, the eyes turn into two black holes, and you have accidentally drawn a skull," says Pflug, which sounds rather appealing to me. He also ended up drawing the cartridge's title screen by hand, pixel by pixel, which took a lot of work - so much that he quickly abandoned plans to include an entire museum hall with display cases. And on some days, nothing he tried worked at all. "That is rather the point of building on hardware this old," he notes. "It makes you earn every screen."
"That is rather the point of building on hardware this old. It makes you earn every screen" -Marcel Pflug

In the end, as he tells me when we chat over email, it took several years of tinkering before he finally cracked it; squeezing the entire archive onto an actual Game Boy cartridge. His handiwork is also available as a ROM you can download for free and then put onto a cartridge yourself if you have the means. Slot it into a Game Boy and you'll be provided with a searchable archive of everything you might ever want to know about Nintendo's debut handheld console. Curious about its innards or the accessories that were released for it? What about the games, the merchandise, even the advertisements? The Game Boy museum has you covered. Pflug calls it "a proper little encyclopedia of the Game Boy's world that you read chapter by chapter like a paperback". I think that's a lovely description, though it's more of a hardback in actuality.

"It is a homage to the machine," Pflug elaborates in his write-up, "and a small attempt to keep this knowledge where it came from in the first place, on the Game Boy itself, so that whatever happens to websites and servers and me, the little grey brick can still tell you its own story." That feels like a particularly relevant sentiment in 2026, when the world is on the cusp of an AI makeover, or perhaps takeover, and when projects such as these are theoretically achievable in minutes rather than years.

How long the project took to complete, Pflug isn't able to easily calculate, because it apparently "came together over many evenings and weekends across several years", with significant gaps in between. He builds things as a hobby when he has the time and the inclination: this isn't his day job, nor his only project. He has a fairly important-sounding corporate role and he also runs a free guitar portal called Sticky Tunes in his spare time. That's alongside a passion for being out in nature, and they all compete for his attention, so there's never quite enough time to go around.

"The truth is that programming and tinkering relax me," he says. "They let me forget the world for a while. And since - if we are honest - nobody has been waiting almost 40 years for the particular solutions I chase, there is something very freeing about it: I am doing it purely to satisfy my own curiosity and to challenge myself." And doing something for the sake of doing it, for the pleasure of doing it, feels like a fierce forehand return against the expediency of AI-generated results if ever I've heard it.
"It carries the feeling of a whole generation, the way a Walkman or a particular pair of trainers does" -Marcel Pflug

Pflug's Game Boy project feels proudly human in the face of AI, which I admire, and I tell him so when we speak. "For me, the Game Boy is not just a handheld," he offers by way of explanation, "it carries the feeling of a whole generation, the way a Walkman or a particular pair of trainers does for people who grew up then."

It's now been several months since Pflug's account of the Game Boy project first surfaced, and I was keen to hear how the world had responded to it since then. "The reaction surprised me," he reveals, "in the nicest way." He was especially warmed to see the project spread beyond the English-speaking parts of the world, all the way to the Game Boy's birthplace in Japan. "That it resonated at the source felt like a small gift," he says.

The Game Boy Museum cartridge project is essentially finished at this point, barring a few small twiddles, but the work doesn't ever entirely cease. Pflug plans to update the build "at least" once a year to keep it current with the Game Boy Museum's archive, "so the little cartridge grows as the game does". Nor is this the end of Pflug's Game Boy adventure; although the cartridge project has wound down, the lessons he learnt making it have led to something else - something equally unexpected. A second cartridge: the GB Test Lab.

"It does the opposite of a game," Pflug explains. "You slot it into a Game Boy and it examines the console itself. It can name the exact cartridge slot contact or memory bit that misbehaves; measure how worn the buttons are; test the printer and the link port. The idea is to give the people who collect, restore, and repair these machines something genuinely useful." People, in other words, like him.

Pflug says he's also learnt a lot about the Game Boy Printer while wrestling with QR codes, so he's working on another tool that turns it into a "a proper label printer". Why? Well, why do anything? To learn, to connect with other people doing the same, to honour something you like. To be human; to be curious.

- Nintendo's making a mini Game Boy music player with collectible Pokémon Red and Blue music cartridges

articles.headline: Oh no, what happened to my OOHPod? Windows command prompt puts in a surprise appearance
keyFacts: An OOHPod postal locker screen in Ireland displayed a Windows command prompt instead of the normal interface during parcel retrieval.
A reader told The Register that tapping the screen opened the prompt, but no keyboard or port was available.
Another tap on the touchscreen restored the normal interface, allowing packages to be collected as usual.
body: The Windows command line is a marvelous thing, beloved by administrators, but not quite so welcome when you're trying to get a parcel out of a locker. Today's example of Windows behaving badly comes from Ireland and one of the nation's OOHPod postal lockers. An eagle-eyed Register reader, trying to retrieve a parcel, found the locker screen instead teasing a command prompt. For the uninitiated, OOHPod is a service where people retrieve and deposit goods in lockers. Scan your ID (or enter it on a touch screen) and the appropriate locker door springs open and the item (or items) can be retrieved. This all works, assuming whatever is running behind the scenes isn't having a bit of a moment, as our reader experienced. Instead of a welcoming display on the locker's screen, our reader found a blank screen and what looked suspiciously like a minimized command-line window. "I tapped to maximize the window," they told us, "and a sudden command prompt appeared immediately afterward." A command prompt? More like an open invitation for mischief for the average Register reader. After all, while ordinary customers might have been flustered, this was surely an opportunity to teach the engineers who allowed it a lesson. Perhaps a cheeky FORMAT, or possibly the creation of a truly cursed batch file? Or something worse? This is surely what the comment section is made for. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your perspective), no pop-up keyboard appeared for our reader to unleash havoc (not that they would dream of such a thing), and there was no handy socket to plug in a peripheral. The touchscreen accepted another finger jab, and the command window went away, replaced by the usual OOHPod interface, allowing packages to be collected as normal. It was the responsible thing to do, and the bank of lockers was left in a state where the next customer would not have to worry about what this odd cmd.exe thing was all about. However, the question remains. Would you have been so responsible? Or, if there was some way to enter commands, would you have tried to turn a minor bork into a life lesson for the engineer who let Windows give passersby a glimpse of its undercrackers? ®

articles.headline: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base
keyFacts: A deadly incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright sparked a major fire that killed and injured people, Canada's defense minister said.
The incident affected many military personnel and overwhelmed regional hospitals with injured patients, officials and a doctor reported.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is investigating the incident to determine what happened, according to the defense minister.
body: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base

EDMONTON, Alberta — Canada's defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.

It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km (120 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

articles.headline: Fire breaks out after deadly incident at Canadian military base, officials say
keyFacts: Defense Minister David McGuinty said people were killed and injured in an incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright that caused a major fire.
McGuinty stated that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating the active and delicate situation while authorities coordinate the emergency response.
McGuinty said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
body: Canada's defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire.
"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," Defense Minister David McGuinty said.
The incident occurred at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located about 112 miles southeast of Edmonton.

"We are dealing with a serious incident at CFB Wainwright, and are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities," said Gen. Jennie Carignan, chief of the defense staff for the Canadian Armed Forces, in a social media post. "Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community, and my thoughts are with all those affected by this incident."

McGuinty did not provide casualty figures or details about what caused the incident. He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate."

The Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, he said. The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support.

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire crossed the base's fence earlier Saturday and was spreading rapidly due to high winds. Firefighters from multiple jurisdictions were responding, and no evacuation order was in effect.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
McGuinty said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
Carney said the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. He said he and Smith were in close contact, as were their ministers and officials.
Smith thanked first responders and those providing care and support to those affected.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
Neither Carney nor Smith provided details about what caused the fire or whether anyone was injured.
The fire came days before the province is set to vote on beginning a process that could lead to its seeking independence from Canada.

articles.headline: Democrats take edge on mail-in ballots in key midterm races
keyFacts: Democrats hold 54% of early and mail-in votes compared to 30% for Republicans, according to state election data compiled by TargetSmart and NBC News.
University of Kentucky political scientist Stephen Voss stated that Democrats have an enthusiasm advantage, though the final outcome depends on overall voter behavior.
Former President Donald Trump encouraged supporters in a video message to utilize early voting, mail-in ballots, or in-person voting.
body: Democrats are running up lopsided majorities of the early votes as Americans head to the polls and mail in their ballots, carving out a clear majority of the votes cast so far.
Of early and mail-in voters, 54% were Democrats, 30% Republicans and 16% independents or “other,” according to state election data compiled by TargetSmart and NBC News.
The early vote advantage carries over to the marquee Senate races, including several held in Republican-leaning states.
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is battling former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the Democratic edge is 55-36%, based on voters’ registrations.
In Iowa, where Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) is in a tough race with Democrat Josh Turek, the edge from registered Democrats is 57-29%, with 14% from “other.”
None of the data show how people actually voted – just who showed up or sent in their ballot.
“We know the Democrats have the enthusiasm advantage,” said University of Kentucky political scientist Stephen Voss.
But what remains to be seen is whether the early numbers point to a predicted overall wave of voters or merely “upper status voters who always vote anyway,” he added.
One way to explore that is to compare numbers to four years ago.

In Republican-leaning Nebraska, where Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts is battling independent Dan Osborne, the Democratic edge has expanded from then. It’s 45-38 now, compared to 44-41 at this point in voting in 2022.
Eighty-nine percent of Democrats who have voted in Nebraska also voted in 2022 and 2024, while 10% are new voters, according to the secretary of state.
For Republicans, 91% voted in the past but just 7% are new voters.
Virginia is seeing a flood of early turnout, with 519,000 ballots in compared to 260,000 by this point in 2022, with the total doubling in left-leaning Fairfax County.
In Texas, the which features a high-profile race between Democratic state Rep. James Talarico (D-Texas) and AG Ken Paxton (R-Texas), Democratic edge is an overwhelming 62-32%.
Democrats historically tend to vote early or by mail, although President Trump has regularly blasted mail-voting in favor of in-person voting on Election Day, calling it “inherently corrupt.”
But this year, on campaign stops and online, he has been changing his message.

In a video last weekend, Trump told supporters from the Oval Office: “If your state has early voting, do not wait. Go out and vote. Vote early, vote by mail, or vote in person on Election Day, November 3rd, so we can defeat the radical left ‘Dumocrats’ in a midterm victory that is too big to rig.”
He also told voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

articles.headline: Dev Behind Russian Roulette Drinking Game Cancels Steam Demo Plans Following AI Copycat Concerns
keyFacts: Alliance Arts canceled the public Steam demo for the game Drunken Goddess Reflux over concerns about potential AI-generated copycats.
The developers said that releasing a public demo could allow others to quickly produce imitating works using AI tools ahead of the game's launch.
Alliance Arts will replace the public demo with a closed online play session and the full game remains scheduled for a December 8, 2026 release.
body: The developer behind Russian roulette anime game Drunken Goddess Reflux has canceled its plans for a public Steam demo, citing concerns over potential AI copycats.

Alliance Arts and Who You's path to launch has seemingly been mostly bump-free since it was announced back in April. Featuring ghostly pinks and purples and a gameplay premise described as "shot glass Russian roulette with a demon who loves you enough to kill you," the recent reveal that it would launch this December only made its future feel clearer.

Part of that release date announcement included the promise that a demo would launch October 19, but as explained in an update post on Steam , those plans have changed. What was originally intended to be a public release for the Drunken Goddess Reflux demo has now been canceled in favor of a "closed play session for a limited number of participants." It's a last-minute move Alliance Arts apologized for, but its concerns related to rapidly advancing AI technology were simply too great to ignore.

"We are concerned that, based on the content of the demo, works imitating or replicating this game's presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI or other tools and released ahead of the game's launch," the developers said in their list of concerns.

In other words, sending a demo out into the wild could open the door for nefarious individuals to use AI to generate a low-effort clone or copycat experience. For a team hoping for a successful launch in just a few months, someone coming in to steal its thunder could potentially throw a wrench into things.

Alliance Arts' fears emerge amid a time when AI is seeping into the gaming industry in ways most may not have ever expected. For example, mods – including mashups of Elden Ring and Super Mario 64 or Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 and Skate – have regularly gone viral on social media in recent weeks. With the controversial technology expanding in new, unforeseen ways every day, it's a risk the Drunken Goddess Reflux weren't willing to take.

Another bullet point concern listed in its message detailed restrictions on posting and streaming gameplay videos, but as the team explained, they "are not currently in a position to properly handle and manage those restrictions." With limited resources to keep nearly unrestricted access to a demo in check, Alliance Arts is moving forward with that closed demo.

"We will therefore hold online play sessions in a closed environment," the developer added, "open to those who have reviewed and agreed in advance to the participation requirements and the rules on posting and streaming gameplay videos."

Players interested in trying the demonic drinking game out were encouraged to join the Discord server presented in the Steam post. Otherwise, Drunken Goddess Reflux is still scheduled to launch on PC via Steam December 8, 2026.

articles.headline: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
keyFacts: Meta updated its commercial terms to state it could use business account domain content to train AI models.
Legal experts expressed concern that the provision allowed Meta to scrape publisher websites for AI training.
Meta removed the language after stating the terms were meant only for ads and business products.
body: Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

body: Underground horror director Jeremiah Kipp has passed away, according to his partner Lindsay Katt. Confirmed through The Long Island International Film Expo, Kipp released his largest movie just earlier in the year, an adaptation of the hit indie horror game The Mortuary Assistant.
“Jeremiah was a gentle soul who was always generous with advice and sharing his knowledge of cinema,” writes the Film Expo, “he leaves behind many friends and an important legacy.”

Based on the 2022 video game, The Mortuary Assistant follows Rebecca (Kingdom Heartâs Willa Holland), a down on her luck woman hoping her new job will pave the road to recovery. Working grim but seemingly benign shifts at the morgue, she suddenly finds herself subject to strange visions. Thatâs when her employer, Raymond (Boardwalk Empireâs Paul Sparks), delivers the bad news. It seems a demonic spirit hitched a ride on one of the cadavers, and Rebecca will need to follow specific rituals to rid herself of the entity.

15 years ago Jeremiah Kipp made my dreams come true. I had a very dark and personal story about Suicide and he believed it needed to to be told. “Jeremiah brought his singular voice and passion to Dread through SLAPFACE and THE MORTUARY ASSISTANT,” posted the studio. “Our love and condolences are with Jeremiahâs family, friends, and collaborators.”

Shocked by his sudden passing, the New York horror movie community is mourning a man they describe as fostering with his time, passion and know-how. Before Assistant, Kipp filmed an array of indie nightmares, from shorts to Shudderâs Slapface in 2021. According to Deadline, the director had just wrapped production on Faceless, an upcoming horror feature based on Cambodian folklore.

The Mortuary Assistant was a crossover hit for publisher DreadXP, who had charmed indie scare fans with their Dread X collections but broke containment on the horror simulator hybrid. While it hasnât made as many waves as other recent adaptations like Iron Lung, it seems it performed well enough to assure the publisher. articles.headline: No further action against government adviser's wife over Palestine Action post, police say
keyFacts: Metropolitan Police officers determined that a social media post by Sarah Helm referencing Palestine Action did not meet the criminal threshold.
Police stated that no further action will be taken regarding the post made by the wife of the government's national security adviser.
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025, making support for the group a criminal offence.
body: - Published
Police say no further action will be taken against the wife of the government's national security adviser after she posted on social media referencing Palestine Action.
Sarah Helm, who is married to Jonathan Powell, wrote on X on Thursday: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support the proscribed organisation.
On Saturday, the Metropolitan Police said Helm's post was "assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold".
"No further police action will be taken," the force added.

On Friday, the Met Police had said it was "in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required" after it was "made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action".
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025. Support of the group is a criminal offence and punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Best-selling author Rooney said she would donate earnings from her books to the group, which has a stated goal of "ending global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".
As a result, Rooney's publisher, Faber, determined it could not sell her novels, including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, in the UK.

articles.headline: Plug-in solar is legal in these 10 states now – how it could save you money
keyFacts: Ten states, beginning with Utah, have legalized backyard and plug-in solar systems for residential use.
Plug-in solar lowers electric bills, but utility opposition and home wiring concerns keep it illegal in many states.
About two dozen states are considering legalization bills, with some advancing and others stalled until the 2027 legislative session.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Multiple states are working to legalize backyard solar setups.
- After Utah, nine other states have legalized it, or are working on bills for plug-in solar.
- 24 other states are stalled but already working on legislation.

Plug-in solar systems are easy to set up and can save consumers money on their power bills, but they’re still illegal in many states. Utah was the first to legalize backyard and plug-in solar, but other states have since caught on, and more are working on their own pathway to legalization.

As we’ve covered before, these plug-in solar setups (also commonly called “backyard solar”) are plug-and-play systems consisting of one or more solar panels, an inverter, and a battery. The system connects to a home’s standard 120-volt outlet, automatically routing solar-generated electricity from the battery to the nearest running appliance.
More from ZDNET
What states have legalized plug-in solar?

Ten states have already legalized backyard and plug-in solar systems, so residents there can already purchase and install systems like the EcoFlow Stream in their homes. Here’s the current status of the states that have already successfully passed legislation, legalizing such devices for consumer use.
Data sourced from Solar.com.
What states are working to legalize plug-in solar?

About two dozen states are still in the process of legalizing plug-in solar. Some bills have stalled until the next legislative session reconvenes in 2027, while others are going through committee hearings.

Balcony solar bills H.5175 and S3143 are advancing in Massachusetts, and the SUNNY Act is pending governor approval in New York. Bills in other states like Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, and Washington, DC have reached committee hearings.

Most states have stalled plug-in solar bills until the next legislative session in 2027, including Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina, and Oklahoma.

Unfortunately, plug-in solar bills have failed in Georgia, New Mexico, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming, so if you live in one of those states, these kinds of devices are technically illegal to operate. This doesn’t mean that it won’t eventually clear the legislative slate in these states, but lawmakers will need to file a new bill to reintroduce them after making necessary revisions.
Can I set up my solar panels if my state legalizes plug-in solar?
Whether you can immediately set up your balcony solar panels or not after the systems are legalized in your state will depend on your home situation.

Generally speaking, the bills in question focus on preventing utility companies from blocking plug-in solar projects. These bills can’t preempt bans on these systems by landlords or HOAs, though supplementary bills have been introduced in some states to include protections for HOAs and landlords.
Why is plug-in solar illegal?

Plug-in solar is illegal because the electrical systems in traditional American homes aren’t designed to receive power from a standard wall outlet. Rooftop solar systems are professionally installed and designed so the energy harvested by the panels flows through a circuit breaker and into your outlets. Plug-in solar, in turn, introduces electricity directly into an outlet, bypassing the electrical panel.

In a plug-in solar setup, nearby appliances draw energy supplied by the breaker and the solar inverter, but the wiring could carry more current than the breaker alone would allow before it trips. But it’s not solely about safety.

Installing your own solar panels means less reliance on local utilities. These companies are the biggest regulatory obstacle for plug-in or balcony solar setups. Their rules and regulations on solar energy are designed for rooftop panels, not plug-and-play systems, so legislation should push utility companies to change that.

There’s also the elephant in the room: utilities would make less money off their services if plug-in solar becomes widely popular. When consumers purchase less electricity, they contribute less to grid costs.
